the Minister of Finance that early last fall an arrangement was made between the Canadian Wheat Board and the railways, an arrangement to which the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Finance were parties, that the railways would be completely free to haul as much grain as possible into export position as quickly as possible.
The result is that the railways have now hauled all of the short haul grain. If the grain has been hauled from the points closest to the west coast, surely it is normal to expect that the grain that is left is going to take more time to haul per car load or per train load, as the case may be, because the distances involved are greater. Looking at the over-all performance of the railways suggests to me that we are going to have a great deal of difficulty in meeting the commitment of some 600 million bushels for export by the end of this crop year. I say that in spite of the repeated hopes expressed in the house by the minister and expressed outside the house by the railway company officials with respect to meeting the target of 600 million bushels by the end of the crop year. The easiest part of the task of moving the grain has been done. Now the long haul grain remains to be shipped.
That is not the whole story. The fact is that there has been terrible discrimination with respect to equalizing quotas on the prairies. To say that what has been done has been done simply for the purpose of getting the largest total volume into export position in the shortest time is not a satisfactory answer. If that type of program had been followed, then since December 14 when the locks at Sault Ste. Marie were closed the greatest movement of grain into export position should have been from southern Alberta, the grain growing area nearest to Vancouver.
However, Mr. Chairman, there has not been a substantial increase in quotas in that area since the Great Lakes navigation season closed. I agree with the sentiment expressed by the Minister of Finance when he hopes that the grain will be moved and that the program will be carried out. However, when one looks at the over-all picture objectively, looks at the performance of the railways in the past, and notes what has happened in the last two and a half months it does not seem to appear that the Canadian Pacific is making great efforts to meet its commitments even in following the program it claims it is following.

I think the Minister of Finance will have to agree that the wheat board has been under severe criticism by some farmers in western Canada with respect to the failure to meet quota targets. That is not the fault of the wheat board at all. As the hon. member for Qu'Appelle mentioned a few minutes ago, the Canadian Wheat Board has no authority to direct the Canadian Pacific to set off railway cars at any specific shipping point. The wheat board may encourage the railway and the Board's officials may have meetings with the railway but there is no authority to give instructions to the railway to set off X number of cars at any particular shipping point.
I sincerely believe that the Canadian Wheat Board has been frustrated in its efforts to equalize quotas and to do justice to the low quota shipping points. I believe this situation has been brought about as a result of the failure of the railways to set off cars at particular points where the Canadian Wheat Board has placed shipping orders. I think that the minister would be doing a service not only to the Canadian farmers but also to the Canadian Wheat Board if he would state that the Canadian Wheat Board has no authority in this respect. I think it would also be helpful if there were a concerted effort by all ministers on the treasury benches, including the Minister of Agriculture, the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Transport, to inform the railways that they were not satisfied with their performance to date. That seems to be the only kind of action that will produce the results needed.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
Finally, Mr. Chairman, may I say that we have had enough of this buckpassing. I am not accusing the Minister of Finance but there has been buckpassing from the railway companies to the terminal elevators and to other people involved in the grain trade with regard to who is responsible for the situation. I think the suggestion made by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle that all these people ought to be called together to try to solve the problems and find the bottlenecks with respect to the grain trade is a good one.
The minister has stated that a co-ordinating committee was set up. I hope the committee has been doing good and useful work. Unfortunately no reports have been issued to the farmers of western Canada about what the committee has been doing and what it has found. Nobody knows anything about it. It would certainly help the morale of the farmers of western Canada, who have been
March 1, 1966

almost completely without income in the last six or seven months, if they knew that somewhere, somebody, be it the Minister of Finance or this committee, was making a sincere and genuine effort to solve the problem of congestion.
I do not intend to comment on lost sales. It seems to me this is something we would not like to see happen again, if we indeed have lost opportunities to make large additional exports of wheat. But I shall not comment on that point at length for this reason. Even without these additional sales we have plenty of deliveries to meet in regard to sales already made. The greatest need at the moment is to deliver wheat to customers who have already bought it.
One suggestion made earlier in the house was that a traffic controller should be appointed to enable better co-ordination between the various agencies involved in moving the grain. If the present situation does not improve soon we should probably take a day to discuss this matter although, goodness knows, we are running short of time in which to carry out our normal work pertaining to estimates and other matters. But I think the situation is sufficiently serious for us to set up a traffic control officer and give him the support he needs.
It is not enough for the government to say: We intend to keep our hands off the wheat board; we intend to keep our hands off the railways. The performance has not been satisfactory. I would agree with the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Transport that if everything was going along reasonably well it would be desirable that the government should leave the C.P.R., the wheat board, the terminal elevators and all others concerned to do the job as best they could. But we can point to hundreds of shipping points in western Canada where quotas and deliveries are lower than they have been at this date for many years past. This in itself is sufficient indication that the result of the whole operation is not satisfactory. I hope the minister will continue his efforts and that he will be a little firmer with the railroads. C.P.R. shipping points in particular show that the company has not been performing as well as we have a right to expect and certainly not up to the level of last year or the year before.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to refer to remarks made by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, the former minister of agriculture, with regard to the shipping of grain. In a small way the question of grain 23033-125J
Supply-Finance
shipments made an impact on me during the time he was minister and subsequently.
The present government was elected in April of 1963. At that time the port of Vancouver was blocked with vessels waiting to get to the grain jetties and load grain. There were between 13 and 15 vessels swinging at anchor in the harbour. They were there for everyone to see. In the latter days of that election compaign the concentration of these vessels had been building up and catching the attention of everyone in the city of Vancouver. This is a sight which no one in Vancouver can avoid seeing if he moves round the city at all.
A general uneasiness begins to take hold in the city as people watch this sight and ask: What is the trouble? Is it due to labour or to the grain elevators or to the harbours board? Just what is it that is causing this build-up and thwarting the efforts of Canadians to send their wheat to the markets they have secured?
We heard this afternoon from the hon. member for Qu'Appelle. He told us how he had gone to those responsible for the movement of grain in the port of Vancouver and discussed with them the means by which the harbour could be unplugged and these ships could be kept moving. He told us how he brought together these various agencies at a meeting and asked them what could be done about it.
When I came here in April, 1963, there fell into my hands a memorandum which the agencies in Vancouver had supplied to the hon. gentleman, the former minister of agriculture. It contained suggestions as to what could be done to improve grain traffic in the port of Vancouver. There were many suggestions made.
It was suggested, for example that the jetties should be lengthened to allow bigger ships and in some cases two ships at a time to dock. There were suggestions that the draft alongside various jetties be increased so that more ships could use these jetties. There were suggestions for improving the cleaning machinery, the drying machinery, the elevating machinery. All these suggestions were made to the minister in an effort to see what could be done to speed this trade. I am referring to the memorandum which was sent to him in 1961.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle had two years or more in which to do something about that memorandum before the government changed. What did he do about it? He

March 1, 1966
Supply-Finance
filed it. Big smoke and no fire. I wish to refer now to the annual reports of the National Harbours Board for those years because hey give a good idea of what actually took place after the former minister took this matter in hand and urged all those concerned with moving grain at Vancouver to get along with the business of improving the port facilities so that the government of the day could move the grain more speedily.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)

They did some work on an overpass over some streets. They built a coffee shop on Granville Island. The total sum spent on capital works in that year amounted to $785,000. We find that provision was made for some flax cleaners at No. 3 elevator. We were not handling a great deal of flax. The movement of wheat, not flax, was our problem. So they put their money into providing some flax cleaners at No. 3 elevator. That was the extent of the implementation in that particular year of the memorandum to the hon. member on grain handling.
Meanwhile, what was he doing in Montreal? Capital works in that year in Montreal amounted to $15,322,793. That is what they thought about eastern port facilities as against the three quarters of a million dollars in improvements of all kinds at Vancouver, of which only a small fraction represented improved wheat moving facilities. What did they spend their money on in the city and port of Montreal? It was spent on the construction of grain elevator No. 4 and marine towers in section 56-

Indeed, looking at the report for 1962 we find that the memorandum was catching up with him and something was happening. Capital expenditures in the port of Vancouver that year were $301,942. Meanwhile, at Montreal expenditures on capital account in that year amounted to over $10 million. That is where the funds of the previous government were being spent on harbours at that time. In spite of all he has told us this afternoon, the previous minister of agriculture in the Conservative government did not implement any of the recommendations that were made to him when he went to the city of Vancouver. That is why, when we were elected in April, 1963, vessels were swinging at anchor in the port of Vancouver waiting day after day for an opportunity to load, and we were getting ourselves into the position in which we find ourselves now.
The solutions for overcoming these problems involve enormous undertakings but they were never undertaken or ever dreamt of by the former minister of agriculture. He filed the memorandum. He was all smoke and no fire, and that is where his statement stands today.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have listened with interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra, and it would be interesting to know what amounts have been spent on the port of Vancouver by the present government since it took office. Though there might be some political policy involved, all of us from the prairies are in sympathy with the hon. member in his efforts to get money allocated for the Pacific coast ports. We feel that the future of grain marketing from western Canada largely depends on the Pacific ports and they should receive more attention from governments than they have in the past.
We had quite a spectacle in the chamber today just as we had the other day in watching the Minister of Finance trying to justify the position of the government and his own position as minister responsible during the last three years for the Canadian Wheat Board. They have been an eventful three years but not because of the actions taken by the government or the minister. They have been years of panic and years of inaction so far as grain marketing is concerned. When I say that I give full marks to the government for the recurring wheat sale to China and the
March 1, 1966

new sales made to the U.S.S.R., but I can remember that when we made the first sale to China the Prime Minister, who then sat in opposition, said that Canada was selling on credit to its enemies and at the same time selling for cash to its friends. He tried to discredit our government because of the tremendous wheat sale to China.
The minister has said that the past year has been a difficult one and that he is well satisfied with the results embodied in the final payment announced a few days ago. But I would remind him that this year's prices are from 9 to 17 cents per bushel less than those of the previous year, this in the face of rising costs for farm machinery, rising costs for labour and everything that goes into the cost of production, this in the face of the promise made by the Liberal party in two election campaigns to provide a guaranteed price of $2 per bushel for western grain producers. Instead of getting $2 per bushel western Canadian farmers received Hazen Argue as a senator, and when one considers the loss of 9 to 17 cents a bushel for that privilege I think the government owes the , western farmers something over and above , what they have received during the past l three years.	'
Today the minister made much of the fact that the advisory board had said that producers were getting the idea they were receiving government money. If that is what I understood him to say, I find it very difficult to believe that the advisory committee to the Canadian Wheat Board would make such a suggestion, because the people who have that kind of understanding are not the producers. They are people other than grain producers who think some of the payments represent government money.

I know my hon. friend does not think this is so but many people had that misunderstanding and I am doing my best to clear it up.

any government is giving them anything, certainly not this government.
A number of things are responsibile for the amount of the final payment made this year. First, there was the serious situation with regard to the allocation and supply of box cars. I believe that situation was largely the result of the detached attitude taken by the minister with regard to all matters concerning the Canadian Wheat Board. He likes to tell us it is his job as minister to report on its operations to the House of Commons. We in western Canada, regardless of party, believe the minister has a greater responsibility with regard to the operations of the Canadian Wheat Board.

maintopic: FINANCE, TRADE AND ECONOMIC AFFAIRS CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I say to the minister that he is doing a very poor job when he does not give them that support that will make their work just as effective as it can be. I was about to refer to the open barley quota that was put into effect last fall. Some farmers could deliver 17,000 bushels and others did not harvest a bushel. Elevators became congested and then there was a cutoff of box cars which meant that they could not make deliveries of the barley they had in stock. There has been an inequitable allocation of space to farmers in different areas of Canada and all because the minister wanted to do something during that period to indicate that grain was moving freely on the prairies under a Liberal government.
Another point with which I should like to deal is that I have heard nothing from the government or the minister about any machinery which has been set in motion to try to bring about some cohesive thinking on the part of the government as it prepares to embark upon the next International Wheat Agreement negotiations. That is something which should be receiving attention at the present time and which should have been receiving attention during the last year or more. It is one of the failures of the government that it has not given the leadership that is necessary in that respect.
I should like to refer also to the ports on the Pacific coast and support a couple of speeches which have been made in the house during

March 1, 1966
Supply-Finance
this session with regard to the development of those ports. We on the prairies endorse the stand these members have taken that the government of Canada should allocate more money to the development and improvement of these ports. I know that criticism may be levelled against what has been done in the past, but let us go back and take a look at 1961, 1962 and 1963. The China wheat agreement had been signed and hon. gentlemen opposite, then in the opposition, questioned whether it was anything more than a onetime deal. What would they have said at that time had the government of the day embarked upon considerable and widespread development of the ports on the Pacific coast in the face of the assertions made by them during the course of the debate in those days

they even convinced me of the possibility-that perhaps the China wheat agreement might not be renewed, although in our hearts and minds we hoped that that agreement would pave the way for sales that would continue for many years to come?
The inaction, if there was any inaction at that particular time, is no excuse for the inaction since that time when the hon. gentlemen opposite have been in office and have had the assurance of recurring sales not only to China but to other nations across the Pacific.
Another matter which should be dealt with is the increase in the loss to farmers ranging from 9 cents to 17 cents a bushel. We all know how it started. It started when the minister panicked and did not support the Canadian Wheat Board the way he should have in the face of what he thought was competition from Australia, competition which has evaporated as a result of events which have taken place.
When you take a look at this whole situation and the grain which has moved in the markets of the world during the last two years you cannot come to any other conclusion but that price has not been a factor in the movement of grain during the entire period. The loss to Canadian farmers, ranging from 9 to 17 cents a bushel, is only part of the loss to Canada as a nation, as the hon. member for Qu'Appelle outlined this afternoon, with regard to meeting the balance of payments situation that this country is faced with at the present time.
As these are the estimates of the Minister of Finance I should like to deal for a minute with the balance of payments situation. I wish to refer to an article in Business Week
[Mr. Nasserden.l
of February 19, 1966. The article is captioned "The Lessons of Power Politics":
At first reading, the U.S. balance of payments figures for 1965 look impressive. They show that the deficit in this country's international transactions was cut to $1.3 billion last year, about half that of 1964 and the lowest deficit in eight years.
Quite a co-incidence when you take a look at the figures in the last eight years. A second look at the figures is anything but reassuring. The article goes on to say:
-arguing that the U.S. should continue to run a deficit indefinitely to finance European expansion and international trade. . . . But in the world of international power politics every dollar that leaves the U.S. lessens our power and increases the hold that our creditors have on us.
That is the United States of America talking.
The massive dollar balances now held by the Europeans can and will be used to force concessions from the U.S. not just in monetary affairs but in foreign policy.
Then they go on to say:
As long as the U.S. has this fishhook planted in its gullet, those with whom we have to bargain always can jerk the line. The only way we can regain our freedom of action is to close the deficit before we weaken our position still further.
If that is true of what could happen in the United States, how much more true is it of Canada today with the alarming increase in the deficit in respect of our balance of payments? It is for the government of the day to try to protect against this problem. We on this side of the house have the satisfaction of knowing that our ministry and the prime minister of that day were able to make inroads into the problems which existed at that time. But some of the measures or policies that had been efficient were allowed to fly out the window by the panic and inaction of members opposite, particularly the Minister of Finance in respect of his attitude concerning grain sales.

Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention to unduly prolong the debate but in view of the course of action that was followed by the minister on Friday in his refusal to face the House of Commons and allow comments to be made on the final price of wheat for the previous crop year I feel I must make a few remarks today. The minister offered a very vacuous excuse for deciding to table the order in council rather than read it as has been the practice in the past in the House of Commons so that opposition members would have an opportunity to comment either favourably or unfavourably on the contents of the particular order in council.
[DOT] (6:00 p.m.)
Everyone knows that the real reason the minister did not make a statement, as has been the custom, is that he refused to face up to his responsibilities as the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board. The reason he gave us was that he was trying to cut short the amount of time he uses in the house. He was not worried about that last year when the final price was the highest on record. He was not worried about making a statement on behalf of the Canadian Wheat Board in respect of the Russian sale or the renewal of the China contract. He does not seem to be worried about taking the credit for those things that sound good.
The unhappy thing about the minister is that he refuses to take the responsibility for those things for which he is responsible and for those things which are not so good. He cannot have it both ways. He must either be the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board, answer questions on behalf of that board and accept his responsibility or pass that responsibility on to someone else.
The hon. member for Medicine Hat, as near as I could follow him, suggested that the minister should take credit for all those things that are good but never take the blame for anything that is bad. I suggest that this is not the kind of attitude that we can stand for in this house.
The minister strove very valiantly to convince the house about the situation in respect of the price of wheat during the years 1957 to 1963 and I noticed that members opposite pounded their desks every time he referred to those years. However, I think it should be
Supply-Finance
pointed out that when we assumed office in 1957 the price of wheat was $1.60 per bushel but as a result of the course of action followed by the party of which I am a member the price of wheat was gradually increased to $2 per bushel. That is what the price was when we left office in 1963. It did not appear to us during that time that there was any great difficulty in holding the price at that level in view of the markets that existed, the demand that had been created and the fact that our surplus had to all intents and purposes virtually disappeared.
What happened following that year? As was pointed out earlier by the hon. member for Rosthern, the government panicked and refused to assist the Canadian Wheat Board in dealing with the United States regarding the cut in prices. The minister has come to the house time and time again and said that he did not want to take credit but that the wheat board should have the credit. Yet at the same time he makes all the announcements. The only announcement he refused to make was that of last Friday, because he knew there would be criticism levelled as a result of his inaction and failure to support the Canadian Wheat Board which resulted in a drop in the price of wheat.
The very fact that the price of wheat is again climbing to the level it was in 1963 is all the proof needed to support the suggestion that the price should not have dropped in the first place. Just a little action on the part of the minister would have saved the farmers of western Canada some $70 to $80 million. Yet the minister had the stupid audacity to say: Well, they have enough money anyway.

Mr. Chairman, I should again like to deal for a moment with the impression that the farmers in the west thave at this time so far as the Canadian Wheat Board is concerned. As the former minister of agriculture pointed out, prior to 1957 there was a great deal of dissatisfaction with the Canadian Wheat Board. The dissatisfaction arose because of the attitude of hon. gentlemen opposite in refusing to accept the responsibility that is theirs to answer to the House of Commons on behalf of that Crown agency. The fact is that the only way the Canadian Wheat Board has of reporting to parliament is through the minister and unless the minister is prepared to accept that responsibility the farmers are going to misunderstand what is the real problem.
We observed quite a spectacle in the house during the spring of the year in which the China grain sale was made. I do not intend to repeat all the statements that were made inside and outside the house in that regard at that time but I do wish to refer to the fact that the Prime Minister said in eastern Canada-I noticed he would not repeat this statement in western Canada-that the China wheat deal was not a good deal, that it was a hoax on the part of the hon. member for Assiniboia of that time. All the time the debate was going on in the house concerning the China grain deal the members of the government party, then on this side of the house, were nitpicking and attempting to find some obscure reason why the credit terms of 
the China wheat deal or the deal itself should not be accepted. In the meantime the farmers of western Canada were pocketing the money that resulted from that sale.
We in the west have had enough of this minister and his failure to do anything to support the Canadian Wheat Board. We have had enough of this rusty Rasputin and his ivory tower on Bay street. The Prime Minister should remove the Canadian Wheat Board from the responsibility of this minister and turn it over to the Secretary of State. She may not know anything about wheat or the wheat board either but at least she is not afraid to get out and attempt to do something.

maintopic: FINANCE, TRADE AND ECONOMIC AFFAIRS CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to take only a few minutes to put forward the three points I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. As a farmer, and I use myself as an example, I have not delivered enough wheat as of this moment to pay last year's fuel bills. One month from now we will be faced with seeding a new crop.
[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
In my opinion this is not a matter of high finance; it should be very simple and there should be no argument about it whatsoever. I have listened to a great deal of talk in the house this afternoon and agree with most of it. I would not agree with one or two things the minister said or with the hon. member opposite who said that there was not time for this sort of thing. I think there is time. When a western Canadian farmer at this time of the year has not delivered enough wheat to pay for last years' fuel, I think it is high time something was done.
I should also like to point out what this situation means in our economy. I borrow money from the bank and pay interest on that money. The wheat board borrows money from the bank to make the initial payments and they pay interest on that money. The elevator companies in turn enjoy the revenue obtained from storage. All these costs are charged to the farmer's account, to my account. The farmer pays interest on the money he borrows, interest on the money the wheat board borrows and pays for the storage. I do not believe it is necessary to be Minister of Finance of a country to add up these costs and realize they take the cream off the crop.
Canadian farmers generally need consideration in this respect, not just western farmers. Western farmers are renowned for their ability to spend their money. Where do they spend it? It is spent in the rest of Canada,
March 1, 1966

particularly in eastern Canada. Western farmers contribute to a very great extent in helping to solve our balance of payments problem.
I have one last point, Mr. Chairman. We do not only have to consider this situation and correct it or bring it to the point where it is acceptable but we have to go one step further and get out of the rut we are in. I say in all deference to the government that we have been in this rut for many, many years because we wait until someone says we can deliver wheat. In our part of the country the C.P.R. has a captive market. If they do not haul grain this month they can haul it next month. The elevator companies have a captive market in regard to storage. I believe we have to break this problem wide open. Hon. members have made suggestions in this regard but I say that to really improve this situation we have to deliver the crop after it is harvested or at least a good part of it. If we do that we will get rid of the three charges which I mentioned and which constitute the real cream of the crop. This would cost nobody anything. The farmer will have an improved price without costing anyone anything and he will have the price he rightly deserves. This can only be achieved through proper management. I submit this suggestion to the Minister of Finance and the other ministers concerned-I see the Minister of Agriculture is here- and I sincerely believe that farmers need this kind of consideration, not only wheat farmers in the west.

There are a few points I should like to make to the minister on the first item of these estimates. I shall refer to them at this time and indicate that we want to hear a great deal more explanation and discussion of these matters during consideration of the subsequent estimates.
One question I wish to raise at this time is the matter of guide lines. The fact that the minister is going to the United States. I want to know whether he is proposing to meet the relevant officials of the American administration to discuss with them further and put before them the very strong resentment that exists in Canada with regard to the effect of these guide lines in this country. It is almost as though the American administration had taken a swipe at something and was unconscious of some of the side effects of its actions in dealing with a problem which we recognize.
We recognize that the United States has a problem in this regard but it must be remembered and re-emphasized, as has been said by my colleague, the hon. member for Northumberland and others on this side of the house, and I am sure this concern is shared by the government, that there are certain considerations that apply to Canada in this connection. We are the best customers of the United States, and if the effect of these guide lines is to stultify the Canadian economy and make it much more difficult for our economy to maintain its progress, of course the Americans are only cutting off their nose to spite their face, although they may not recognize that fact. This is the point I want to emphasize.
[DOT] (6:20 p.m.)
Not only is there the question of the guide lines but also the action of the Securities and Exchange Commission of the United States in their requirement that in Canadian companies where there is a 10 per cent shareholding, I believe it is, in the United States, these companies must make full disclosure as required by the American authorities. I believe this is going rather too far. It will only create resentment in this country. It is not that we have that many Canadian companies operating in the United States where the shareholdings by United States interests may amount to 10 per cent; yet we find Canadian companies are being asked to supply information as to their total operation. We might counter by saying that any United States corporations owned by 1 per cent, 10 per cent

or 15 per cent Canadian interests must disclose to us all of their operations. I am sure that Washington would react very promptly and with a great deal of resentment if we did that. What is fair for them is fair for us. I believe that this action by the S.E.C. is totally uncalled for. It will be the duty of the Canadian government to make these views known to the United States government and to tell that government this is the type of action that is not calculated to improve relations between our countries.
So far as the guide lines themselves are concerned, I think I can only emphasize what has been said on this side of the house. I do not believe the guide lines are innocuous. I think the minister recognizes that perhaps his first indication was that he was taking it all too calmly; otherwise we would not have had the action taken by Mr. Kierans in the province of Quebec and others. Albeit they did use rather unorthodox means of getting their point across, yet they do have a point to get across. That is all I am going to say on this matter.
On February 2 the minister was good enough to file an answer to a question I put on the Order Paper, question No. 100, concerning the results under a supplementary agreement according to the provisions of the Established Programs Act. This was the 1964 Bill No. C-146 which, if I recall rightly, was going through some time in July or August of that year. I remember the hon. member for Davenport, who occupied the portfolio of the Minister of Finance, hailed this particular arrangement as one of the stars in the Liberal heaven.
This bill for the opting out of joint programs was going to be the solution for the relations between the federal government and the provinces in connection with such programs. At the time I indicated, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands indicated and so did some of my other colleagues that this bill was a hoax. There was nothing to it in so far as granting greater fiscal autonomy to the provinces was concerned. The Prime Minister paraded up and down the country saying that this was the new Liberalism. The then Minister of Finance did the same. The proof of the pudding is always in the eating and I am very interested to see that there was only one province that took advantage of the provisions of this bill. Yet it had been designed for the benefit of all Canada because dominion-provincial relations
March 1, 1966

are not the private preserve of the government of Canada and one province. Dominion-provincial relations apply to all provinces, whether on the Atlantic coast, in central Canada or out west.
I assert that in this regard all provinces have their rights and their positions. They stand as equals in fiscal relations. Certainly as a representative from the western provinces in this house I doubly assert that. The detail of the answer given by the minister is immaterial in so far as the quantum of money that will be realized by the province of Quebec under the income tax abatement provided for under the supplementary agreement, but I must insist again on pointing out that as soon as the principal agreements terminate the supplementary agreement falls to the ground and unless there are renegotiations of the original agreement the abatement of income tax goes back to the government of Canada. This has not been a permanent abatement or assignment of these points. The law is patently clear and there is not much more freedom under Bill No. C-146 than there was heretofore. Mr. Chairman, I think the importance of this particular vote is such that a few comments should be made in respect of it. We were pleased the other day when the

March 1, 1966
Supply-Finance
minister announced his intention oi extending the expiry date of the Municipal Development and Loan Board, because had he not I believe many municipalities in the country would have been in difficulty in respect of completing projects which had been started under the provisions of this particular facility. I think the minister and the government of the day should take a real hard look at this particular point before they go into the final decisions regarding the new budget. We regret that this particular loan development fund was not made the beginning of a new approach to the problem of municipal financing.
I note the arguments the minister has put up with regard to the fund; but I think this fund has justified itself by the degree of participation of the various municipalities. The question of municipal financing in this country is the most difficult single problem of public financing, simply because the municipal authorities in particular face an unequal struggle for the tax dollar in so far as being able to finance those services which it is their obligation to provide. It has been true down through the years that some permanent facility should have been established in this regard. If my memory serves me right, I believe it was in 1938 that the municipal development and loans act was passed and in the meantime nothing very much was done to act upon this authority.
Mr. Chairman, unless something is done to assist the cities, towns, counties, municipal districts and villages in meeting the tremendous problem they face in financing the public developments, which basically are those services which it is their responsibility to provide, then we are not going to be able to progress as we should.
I would urge upon the minister and upon the government the necessity of getting down to this particular level of financing so far as the governments of our country is concerned. How can municipalities contend with the demand for schools, the demand for hospitals, the demand for water and sewage facilities, for streets, parks and all the rest when repeatedly they themselves have to go out to the public market, or often to the United States, to borrow money at tremendous cost- a cost which is so great that by the time the payments are amortized the expenditure for the use of the money has at least doubled and sometimes trebled the cost of the project they are seeking to construct. It is in this area that the federal government could do more than

in any other way toward helping the local governments.
We in the Social Credit party for years have recommended that this is the responsibility of public financing. This is not to pay for the services which should be paid for by the taxpayer's dollars, but it is money for the facility that provides those services. That money should be available at lesser cost, and through an easier means than is presently available.
This would tend to lessen the tax burden; it would tend to decrease the cost to the government and leave more money in the pockets of the taxpayers for the essential cost of government at other levels which cannot be provided for in this way. We recommend now that the minister very seriously consider, before we enter into another year, that a permanent municipal loan fund be set up, not as a board but as a separate bank. We have the Industrial Development Bank, a bank which has served a very legitimate purpose in our economy in the post-war years. A bank which originally was intended to provide capital for high risk development and industry which could not obtain capital through the normal channels of finance. This bank has functioned well. It has authority as part of the Bank of Canada to expand its own credit. I believe the record will show that the expansion of its reserves has rendered an effective service. I would suggest, in light of the present financial situation, that the minister would be well advised to take the Industrial Development Bank and transfer it as the municipal development bank so that its credit would be available to the municipal governments for their capital costs.
If the Industrial Development Bank can do what it has been doing in the private sector of the economy, there is no reason why the municipal development bank as part of the Bank of Canada could not render as good a service for public financing. I believe this is one of the greatest needs of our whole financial situation at the present time. It would lift the burden and ease the problem in respect of education. It is evident that in the next ten years we will need $10 billion for school expansion alone. This is the kind of service which could be rendered to the municipal and provincial governments. I would urge the government and the Minister of Finance to take this into serious consideration.
A little while ago the hon. member for Halifax made a sarcastic remark about the debt free money. During the war we were
March 1, 1966

able to get money which was necessary to the country at cost, because of the national emergency. At one time Mr. Ilsley, the Minister of Finance, announced a bank loan for the financing of the war and someone asked how much it would cost. Mr. Ilsley replied that it would cost three quarters of 1 per cent. The hon. member then asked how he could get it at this when he personally had to pay 4 or 5 per cent, and the answer was simply that that represented the actual cost.
[DOT] (7:10 p.m.)
Perhaps you could not obtain money at the cost of three quarters of 1 per cent, but you could obtain it for less than 5, 6 or 7 per cent which is the price being paid for public developments. This is what we are referring to when we say that we should make special provision for another category of money, that for public financing. We do not refer to tax capital or private capital, which ought to come out of our own savings, but to public capital to provide for the tremendous financing need we have in this country for the facilities I have just mentioned.
One of the most important things the government ought to consider in the area of financing, aside from the expected reforms in the way of new legislation which must come in regard to the Bank Act, is the establishment of this new category. If the government gave consideration to the establishment of something of this kind, I believe it would provide a solution to one of our most difficult financing problems. I cannot urge or recommend in strong enough terms to the government that this be done. I am convinced that if some solution such as I have suggested was brought forward many of our financial problems would be solved. If the government does not wish to adopt my suggestion perhaps they could revert to the original 1938 legislation and put that into effect.

Soviet grain production last year fell short of government targets by 30 million tons, a state planning official said yesterday.

Canada's primary role historically in world trade has been one of exporting what we loosely call the raw materials, and of importing the finished products. We find ourselves in this position because of the prominent position of the United States in world affairs, because of the relative size of their population compared to ours, because of its proximity to us, because of the relative wealth of that nation as compared to Canada and because of some factors contained in domestic policy within Canada. It is also estimated that the tax revenues from Expo that the federal and provincial governments together will receive will be more than the deficit is estimated to be. Those are estimates; but the fact of the matter is this is going to be a great institution. This will be the greatest exposition ever staged by any country in the world, and I can say that with confidence because there are many yardsticks to support the statement.
I refer to the number of countries already signed up, the number of tickets sold in advance, and other yardsticks. Based on and judged by the many yardsticks, Expo holds the promise of being the greatest exposition put on anywhere. It should be a matter of signal pride to Canadians and I urge everybody everywhere to get behind this great undertaking and support it in the best tradition of Canadians.

Mr. Chairman, no one will deny that, having been associated with various industries for the past several years, the Minister of Trade and Commerce has acquired a fairly complete experience in that field.
We have before us now the estimates of his department, one that will have cost the Canadian people $82,340,040 for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1966, that is at the end of this month.
Mr. Chairman, I was glad to hear the minister tell us how much he expects, for

Canada, from the world fair which will show a deficit of something like $61 million but which, on the other hand, will bring billions of dollars to Canada and fill the coffers of the various governments-municipal, provincial and federal- with hundreds of thousands, even hundreds of millions of dollars.
That is probably why the minister hopes that the 11 per cent tax on building materials will eventually be abolished. We hope to make a profit with the world fair.
Mr. Chairman, I shall not be long but I should like to draw the attention of the Minister of Trade and Commerce on the balance of payments with the United States and urge him to try to find out why this balance shows a deficit.
The minister has his explanations, so has the government and so have we. We believe that the agencies of the department, which are scattered abroad to promote Canadian goods and products manufactured in Canada for export, do not give the results which we have the right to expect.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
First of all our foreign trade or our sales to other countries seldom bring us any profits. We sell our products much below cost to the United States as well as to other countries. That is undoubtedly why our balance of payments shows a deficit or it might be because we owe more than is owed us especially by our neighbours to the south, the United States.
Mr. Chairman, the minister is undoubtedly aware that our trade with the United States boils down to selling them raw materials. We do not sell manufactured goods to the United States but raw materials, iron from the Un-gava, water from British Columbia or any other natural resources; we sell our raw materials to the United States and at prices lower than production costs.
The United States process those materials and bring them back to Canada as manufactured goods.
A little earlier the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) mentioned it and rightly so. The minister said that was a problem for industry. Well, not primarily; it is definitely a matter related to our foreign trade because the minister undoubtedly knows that if we processed our raw materials in Canada, if we had more secondary industries, for instance in my own region, where we produce copper in large quantities, if we had secondary industries, not only gold, copper or zinc

mines to process those materials, it seems to me that Canada would benefit from it.
It seems to me that we could sell at a better price to the United States and to other countries. Then, our people, our country, Canada, would benefit to a large extent.
I sincerely believe, Mr. Chairman, that Canada is being drained of raw materials by the United States. The United States have to get them here. They have to get iron here. They had to ask British Columbia and the Canadian government for water from the Columbia river. For instance, they will have to ask for water from James Bay and Hudson's Bay for the Great Lakes where the water level drops every year. As a matter of fact, they have already done so. The United States have to come to us.
It does not mean that we should take advantage of the situation, but it means, for instance, and very clearly, that we should at least take advantage of the privileged situation where we find ourselves. And there is no doubt that we are in that situation.
Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that an incentive to the establishment of secondary industries to process our raw production at home, would help considerably, and that the United States would nevertheless come and buy from us finished, or at least, semifinished products which would yield millions and millions of dollars in profits to Canada instead of our having a balance of payments.
Besides, Mr. Chairman, the minister is very well aware of this. As I said a few moments ago, he has undeniable industrial experience. He knows very well that if we had secondary industries in this country, the Canadian people would derive profits from them. Then, we could perhaps consider lowering taxes, lowering the sales tax on building materials, etc.
I do not intend to speak very long on this vote No. 1 of the Department of Trade and Commerce, but I call the Minister's attention to the fact that it is important, and I believe in his good faith and his goodwill to stimulate the creation of secondary industries in this country, not only in Toronto or Montreal, but in other areas, and those areas where the raw materials exist, such a Rouyn-Noranda, or Val d'Or, where there is copper. And the same applies to eastern and northeastern Quebec and to Ungava, to northeastern Ontario, such as Timmins, Cochrane, Kirkland Lake. Everywhere, secondary industries could be created in order to industrialize the country to a greater extent. Such industries

Mr. Chairman, on consideration of the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce, I wish to raise with the minister a problem of great concern to the constituents of the constituency of Sherbrooke, as well as to numerous Canadians. I refer to the recent U.S. decision to cut investments.
A few moments ago, the Minister referred to this in his short speech. I do not have to recall here the mechanism and the background of that decision of the United States which is to remain in force until February, 1967. They are well known.
However, I wish to reflect on what we are told and on what should be done to reduce as much as possible, its bad effects on our country.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce maintains that it is not proven that the American guide lines affect Canadian subsidiaries of American companies.
It should be noted, in the comments of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, that this embarrassment was not openly shown until now, but the minister does not tell us in sufficient detail his concern for the days to come.
Mr. Charles Chartier, general delegate of the province of Quebec to New York, said that until now the measures taken by the United States do not unduly affect Canada and that, for the moment they only diminish temporarily the importance of New York as the capital of international finance.
But this general delegate of Quebec does not specify what present limited effect these measures have on Canada and what would be their future implications.
In an interview given on February 10, 1966 to the New York Times, the premier of Quebec, Mr. Jean Lesage, said that the measures taken by Washington would be harmful to the growth of the province of Quebec.
On the other hand, in addition to denouncing the direct intervention of Washington in the Canadian economy Hon. Eric Kierans, Quebec Minister of Health foresees serious

Supply-Trade and Commerce consequences on the structure and organization of the Canadian economy. He foresees a harmful increase in our trade deficit with the United States, and lower profits for American subsidiaries in Canada. That is the opinion of a responsible man, which creates worry and disappointment.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
Let us study briefly, Mr. Chairman, the concern expressed summarily by Hon. Eric Kierans. He states that the guideline was given by the Secretary to the U.S. Treasury, Mr. Henry Fowler. The American Congress did not study the matter, nor did it enact any law in this regard. American capitalism is controlled by a handful of men who try to achieve the political objectives of the country without consulting Congress.
Mr. Kierans still claims that the decision constitutes foreign meddling in Canadian business and keeps us from being masters in our own home. It is a violation of Canadian sovereignty.
Such decisions, adds the Quebec minister, affect our growth, our development. Before taking them Washington should consult its branch offices, Ottawa and Quebec.
It is clearly up to Ottawa to show all those companies, subsidiaries and others, what their responsibilities are as Canadian citizens, and those are to seek a higher rate of growth, increased efficiency and a more intensive use of our resources and skills. Ottawa is entitled to full explanations as regards changes in the distribution of dividends, in the investment policy and in the purchasing system. Ottawa should also ask for reports on transactions made between Canadian subsidiaries and their American parent companies.
According to the Quebec minister, the Companies Act should be amended in order to redefine the status of private companies. The majority of subsidiaries do not inform the public about their activities in Canada.
In Great Britain it appears that a company is not considered a private company, and therefore exempt from informing the public, if some of its shares or bonds are held by an incorporated company. Canadian-owned companies having to file financial reports are in an unfair position as compared to American subsidiaries which do not have to do so. Of course, this creates unfair competition, concludes the Quebec minister.
There you have, Mr. Chairman, the opinion of a responsible man creating concern and deception.

DEBATES	March 1, 196S
As for the governor of the Bank of Canada, Mr. Louis Rasminsky, he advises against raising prices and production costs without, however, intervening directly in the debate. The situation will be rosy: on the one hand, American investments are refused Canada and, on the other, Canadians will not obtain as much credit from the banks.
Mr. Chairman, the situation is serious, even alarming. What are the government and the minister doing at the beginning of this crisis? Very little, indeed.
We have already begun to feel all the ills we shall experience because of the decision of the United States and the apathy of our government. Allow me to list a few of those ills: hardening of Canada-U.S. relations; increased friction between federal and provincial governments; increase of our discount rate from 4J to 4J per cent; postponement of many works; slowing down of our economic development; increased unemployment; higher prices and costs; increased trade imbalance with the United States; decrease of our exports; financial disturbances in Canada; decrease of fiscal receipts and of per capita income; increased poverty and destitution in Canada.
I admit, Mr. Chairman, that those prospects are not too bright, but it is better to face the situation squarely than to bury our head in the sand.
From the shades of meaning of the remarks made by Messrs. Chartier, Rasminsky, Lesage, Kierans and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters) and in view of the events arising out of the American decision, three facts emerge: (1) Canada's economy, money and finance are too highly dependent upon the United States and to date, our country has not shown enough awareness and foresight in its policy, being often thrown off balance and surprised by decisions of our neighbours to the south.
(2)	Our economic, financial and monetary policy lacks Canadian characteristics and a definite orientation.
(3)	Confronted by policies initiated by other countries, including the United States, our government is timid, easy-going, if not altogether soft, ashamed to complain or to react.
It is not enough to record present and future inconveniences for Canada and to be satisfied with recriminations. The government, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters), the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) and the whole government must act
March 1, 1966

together, with dispatch, and on several fronts simultaneously.
If the minister was unworried as to the consequences upon Canada of the recent American decision, I recommend that he immediately order a study in that connection and that he publish the report at the earliest possible moment. I am inclined to believe that the apprehensions of many Canadians are well founded.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
Mr. Chairman, I would not want to talk too long about a suggestion which seems reasonable to me. According to the president of the Royal Bank of Canada, Mr. W. E. McLaughlin, Canada should contemplate bringing to an end the agreement on our exchange reserves. That might increase slightly the cost of our loans, but we would have free access of the American market and would no longer have to hinder our monetary policy by maintaining our reserves at a pre-arranged level.
With regard to foreign investments, looking for new sources of capital would help us to maintain a better balance. We could go to other European countries who are anxious to invest abroad.
I hope that when he was in France recently, in Paris particularly, the minister had the opportunity to invite the French people and the French businessmen to invest more capital in Canada.
Why not create also in Canada a national investment board to better co-ordinate our long-term needs in capital and find the best places in Canada to use it? We are proceeding at random.
The Bank of Canada should play a more active role in the present economic circumstances by putting more money in circulation to meet additional needs.
Nothing would legally prevent the Bank of Canada from lending money to the provinces and the municipalities at low and preferred rates.
Chartered banks should agree to lending revolving funds to finance enterprises, which would enable them to use their own savings for investments.
If the maximum interest rates now set at 6 per cent were abolished and set up at a more reasonable level this would enable the banks to meet the competition they now face and would reduce the need for many Canadians to borrow from finance and personal loan companies often at excessive and prohibitive rates in some cases.

On the other hand, the government should accept at last to reduce taxes. It would be an encouragement to the taxpayers and the companies.
I would now like to draw the attention of hon. members to an article published in the last issue of The Monetary Times in which the assistant dean of the political science faculty at the Ottawa University invites the government to reduce taxes.
The government should promote personal savings, and in order to encourage Canadians to invest their savings, it would help if an amnesty were granted in the case of legal proceedings taken for money hidden in woollen socks, safety deposit boxes and other secret places.
The restrictions announced by the White House show that it would be advisable to set up an investment agency in Canada. The leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Douglas) has made such a suggestion in the past. I think it deserves serious consideration and should not be brushed aside.
In my opinion, the federal government should take into consideration the suggestions of Hon. Eric Kierans to the effect that a full explanation should be demanded concerning the changes made in the distribution of dividends, the investment policy and the purchase system.
The federal government should redefine, in the light of the American decision, the status of private companies, so that the Canadian people may be informed about the whole financial and administrative setup of the companies established on their territory.
There is one sure thing, Mr. Chairman. Because of the problem raised by the American decision, Canada is faced with a positive challenge. Should we blissfully await the nefarious consequences of this event or should we, on the contrary, make the most of it to secure our economy, our financial system and our trade on a more solid and more flexible basis?
So I ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce to get together with the Minister of Finance and his other colleagues to study my comments and inform at the earliest possible moment, all Canadians who await his intents, his initiatives and those of the government.

Mr. Chairman, I know the minister will listen to a few words from a backbencher or at least a sidebencher in connection with the problem of export trade. I do
March 1, 1966

Supply-Trade and Commerce not want to take up time to belabour the point that has been made time and time again that Canada has to export more manufactured products. I believe the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam once said that we no longer want to be hewers of wood and drawers of water. This is true; we want to export manufactured goods. So does every other country in the world, but with this difference today, Mr. Chairman, that at one time it was very difficult for a new country or for a poor country to acquire the capital with which to purchase equipment, machinery and so on. These capital goods are now readily available from Germany, France, and especially Germany on the never, never plan. We are therefore in very serious competition.
We have two ways of trying to promote an increase of export trade in manufactured goods. One of the ways was the way the present member for Northumberland, a former Minister of Trade and Commerce, expounded. This was by the hoopla method, the great trade fairs, gladhanding and going around the country stumping the idea that businessmen are lazy, that they need to get up and get going and sell. This is a rather archaic method today. Canadian businessmen are not lazy, they are hard working, and they are quite aware of their potential.
However, there are other problems which are difficult for Canadians to overcome. I have been in this business, probably longer than other members, and I have tried exporting. First, we are competing with nations which are well established in the export trade. They have had their export machinery established for 40 or 50 years. They know with whom they are dealing, where they are going to deal and the prices of the types of products. We do not. The establishment of a trade or export department is a very expensive business. Second, the financial set-up in these countries for export trade is much better than ours.
With all respect to GATT, there are countries today which will allow their exporters to sell their products without careful scrutiny, and on which financial institutions paid one hundred cents on the dollar for receivables. In other words, the governments of these countries are absorbing the total risk. We are not. Most important of all, many countries today are using very sophisticated methods of market research, the results of which become available to the exporter and manufacturer. We do not do this. The reason I am making these remarks now is that the

minister, being a new minister and a reform minister, will want to hear what I say and ascertain whether or not it can be introduced by our government.
Let us consider my own case. When I was in business, I naturally went to the Department of Trade and Commerce to find out what the picture was in one of the South American countries. We had the normal statistics given to us, the currency exchange, tariffs, etc. Then of course the balance of the information was to be forthcoming from the trade commissioner when we got to that country. However, we found the trade commissioner, although working hard, did not really know what we were after, did not really know what was available in that country. He was more interested in transferring into the Department of External Affairs. This is another curious thing. When we are depending upon exports, the head of state in just about every country comes from the Department of External Affairs and not from the Department of Trade and Commerce. We have had occasions where a grade eight civil servant has been under the jurisdiction of a grade five civil servant who happens to be from the Department of External Affairs. In other words, there is not enough incentive to stay with the Department of Trade and Commerce. This is something for the minister to consider.
Let me give you an example of a very progressive country which has accepted the more sophisticated methods of market research and applies them to their export trade. I refer to Japan. Some hon. members will have heard of an establishment called JE-TRO, or Japanese Export Trade Research Organization.

Will the hon. member permit an interjection? I think the minister might misunderstand his remarks. He said "head of state", when he meant head of mission. The hon. member is referring in that connection to the head of our mission in each country.

Whether it is the head of state or head of a mission, the point is that the chief man in that country is usually from the External Affairs Department and not from the Trade and Commerce Department.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
In order to continue my illustration, I may say that the Japanese government pays for and obtains careful research for certain products. They find out what Canadians want.
March 1, 1966

They find out through private research organizations in Canada the types of goods that Canadians like; the colour; the weight. They find out the prices we are willing to pay. They go farther than that and they find out who buys the goods, to what clubs they belong and so on. One would be amazed at the detail in these reports. The result is that when a Japanese salesman or representative comes to Canada he knows exactly where to go to sell his goods. An example of this type of research is seen in the fact that Japan now controls 68 per cent of the stainless steelware market in Canada, when she started with only 18 per cent a few years ago. This is sophisticated marketing. If the Canadian manufacturer had this information he would be in a much better position. I would urge the minister therefore to introduce this idea, even if we have to get outside help to advise our trade department, so that we shall develop within our Department of Trade and Commerce an up to date market research branch.
I should also like the minister to consider that there are some fields in which we have an edge. We may not necessarily have to sell goods. Let me illustrate what I mean, for example. We have just about the world's supply of uranium. There are many countries in the world, and South America is a good example, where electric power is not available and will not be available for many years. We have the money, we have the uranium: Can the minister not imagine what we could do if we manufactured right here atomic electric units to provide electricity and then installed them in countries needing power? We do not have to sell this equipment. Even if it cost $10 million we could lease it to countries needing it, and charge so much per kilowatt. Eventually we should establish for ourselves a ready market, and help have-not nations, without a great expenditure of money. There is nothing wrong with the leasing business. I.B.M. made a fortune from the leasing of equipment.
We have the money, we have the men; we have the know-how. We need a new approach, and not necessarily that staid, solid approach which has been used for years and years in our trade relations. I trust that the minister will prove to be what I hope; I trust that he will guide his department into a completely new avenue of endeavour.

Mr. Chairman, I only wish to detain the house for a few minutes. First of all I want to congratulate the minister on his appointment. I may say that if we had to have a Liberal appointed to that post, from that constituency, I am very pleased to see that he was the one to arrive here.
Mr. Chairman, I must admit before I proceed that I shall be speaking here under what I consider undue influence. I was talking to my wife before, and she said to me, "Mind you be careful about what you say, I am very fond of Mr. Winters." As you see, Mr. Chairman, I am rather restricted.
I do want to express my support for the policy announced by the members of this party in connection with this department. I support all efforts to promote greater manufacture from raw materials in Canada, to promote the development of secondary industry, particularly in smaller towns and communities under Canadian ownership. I support this program, which I believe can only be brought about as a result of co-operation between the minister, departmental officials, municipalities, trade unions, farm organizations and other community organizations. I am a great believer in getting the participation of as large a number of people as possible in the advancement of any program. I do suggest to the minister that it would be well worth his time and the time of his officials to promote this participation among the various groups I have mentioned. I also suggest that the minister should as much as possible visit not only the larger centres of Canada, but those centres that are not usually visited by members of the ministry or by his senior officials. I do not intend to delay these proceedings for more than two or three minutes. The hon. gentleman knows that the committee is always easy on a new minister. And he is new to this parliament, although he is still steeped in Liberal lore and tactics from days gone by when we were here together. But we will defer any remarks critical of the minister until his estimates come up the next time around.
We shall not remind him on this occasion of any speeches he has made, since he has been divorced from political matters for about eight years, though we may call to his attention some day a speech he made in 1962. We feel kindly disposed toward him because he is interested in the removal of the 11 per cent sales tax, and his phrase "at the earliest possible moment" means something, I think, to a man of his capacity who is accustomed to getting things done, not just talk about them. So we are resting our hopes on this minister.
I should like to commiserate with him on the situation with regard to his department, the Department of Trade and Commerce, which at one time was one of the largest and most important departments of government. But in his unfortunate absence this department has been emasculated and another department has been set up called the Department of Industry. The Department of Trade and Commerce has suffered accordingly. Now that the hon. gentleman is back in the house, with all his experience, I think the government might seriously consider transferring the Department of Industry back to where it belongs in the Department of Trade and Commerce, and restoring the Department of Trade and Commerce to the position it occupied only a few years ago.
I wish to ask the minister a question or two now with regard to the Export and Import Permits Act. If he is not in a position to answer them tonight he may do so later on. In any case this act comes up for review in June, when it lapses unless renewed.
My question relates to export and import permits as far as Southern Rhodesia is concerned. The Secretary of State for External
March 1, 1966

Affairs relied on this act in order to impose those sanctions. May I ask the minister this: Under section 4 of that act has the governor in council published an order in council adding Southern Rhodesia to the area list, as should be done under this section of the act? I should like to be precise in my answer. Much of this action was taken before I became minister. I should like to take the question as notice and answer it later, if I may.

In the same vein, may I say I was interested in the announcement the minister made today. We know there are three main headings under which this could become operative. He could say that we were likely to become short of copper-he could give that as a reason. Is there a world shortage of copper?

Yes, there is a world shortage of copper, and it has taken on quite serious proportions. Several hon. members who have spoken this evening have quite properly referred to the advantage of processing our own copper in Canada. We have reached the stage where some processors have been unable to get the supplies they require. We therefore took the further step of restricting exports of scrap. As a result we find that scrap is now getting back to the domestic processors.
Some of the concentrate-the ore is a very small part of the picture-is able to find its way towards the London metal exchange. We want to be sure, without interfering at this stage with the normal flow of commerce, that we do have authority under the Export and Import Permits Act to review these contracts

Supply-Trade and Commerce when they come up for renewal. We have extended the date until March 21 so that anybody who has a contract can have it appraised in the meantime. There is not much point plugging one gap if you fail to notice the others. Most of the concentrate produced in Canada does go to Canadian smelters, but some of it is shipped abroad, and some will continue to be shipped outside Canada for economic reasons-the inaccessibility of a smelter, for instance. But we think that in present circumstances this should be under control and review.

One further question on the copper situation. I compliment the minister on having placed scrap copper under export control. As I understand, about 7 per cent of our supply of copper comes from scrap. But why does the minister allow scrap copper to be exported to the United States where it can be made into finished products and then sold on the Canadian market in competition with Canadian producers? To my way of thinking control over exports of scrap copper should include scrap copper sent to the United States. I should like to hear the minister's reasoning.

Well, it has been traditional to have an open border policy with respect to scrap movements to the United States, and United States scrap coming here. If we found there was a significant volume moving we would have to do something about it; but there are no indications that there is very much, if any, copper scrap finding its way from Canada to the United States. Nevertheless we have this under consideration.

In recent years a large amount of our mining development in B.C. has rested upon the interests of a foreign country, namely Japan.
This was recognized not long ago by the Premier of B.C. when he visited Japan and made the comment that possibly B.C. has a greater attachment to Japan than it has to the eastern part of Canada. I am sure he


meant by that, that B.C. in years past has suffered at the hands of selfish interests in eastern Canada, in Toronto in particular, selfish mining interests, who have always wanted to preserve their own position within the economy, wanted to exert their power and authority wherever possible and, as a result, whenever they have been successful, we in the western part of Canada have suffered.
Even though we desire smelters to be built in B.C., even though a smelter would advance us economically and put us in a position of being able to export materials at a higher price than we export our ore and concentrates, and even though moves have been afoot on a number of occasions in the past, dating back to the period just prior to the second world war, we have found those legitimate needs and desires frustrated at every turn because of the interests with which the minister is so intimately associated, the interests in Toronto who want to preserve their own position. Though the minister is shaking his head at what I say, this is the fact of the matter.
If the minister wants to go back to the period at the end of the second world war and make inquiries about the attitude within the department of finance in the province of B.C., when we were on the verge of establishing, or having established an iron smelting industry in B.C., he will find that project was killed before birth because of the interests in eastern Canada who wanted to preserve their position and did not want any upstart western province becoming an industrial section of the nation because they felt it would interfere with their monopoly position in this field.
The minister does not have to take my word for this. He can get this information by searching diligently in the files of his own department and the files of the Department of Finance, and seeing the correspondence which took place at that time with the province of B.C.
We are still in this position. I believe it is correct that if we can participate with other nations in effecting lower tariff barriers we can open up markets for commodities that these tariff barriers were associated with before. However, it seems to me that tariffs were instituted primarily to protect home industries and that their secondary effect was the provision of income to the government which imposed them. However, the tariffs were originally put into effect to preserve the economic positions of the industries associated with the tariff barriers, the feeling being that if the tariff was low enough the industry concerned would be driven out of business by the importation of lower priced articles.
Tariffs are imposed in respect of manufactured products rather than raw materials. If the government feels it has the degree of faith indicated by the minister in the forthcoming tariff negotiations, it should be doing something to bring about an agreement to lower tariffs, and should operate in concert and conjunction with the Department of Industry, and the entire cabinet, to promote as fast as possible the development of secondary manufacturing industries in Canada.
