I did not realize we were going into this department. I thought we were going into the industry section. There is one matter about which I should like to inquire which relates to the Department of Defence Production. I understand that some time ago, a year or two ago, the purchasing of materials for the Indian affairs branch was

taken over by the Department of Defence Production. In talking with Indian affairs branch personnel in the field, in talking with local suppliers of goods and materials that are required by the Indian affairs branch, I have learned, to put it mildly, that they think this system leaves a great deal to be desired. They feel it allows for a great deal of inefficiency and increases the length of time it takes to make deliveries of orders compared with what it used to be under the Indian affairs branch.
In many instances local suppliers of materials are cut out of the picture because the Department of Defence Production has some relationship or liaison with the larger centres for distribution purposes. I do not want to document these instances, and I do not think they need documenting in any event. Some instances have been related to me of misunderstandings over orders which were given. In other instances the materials which are supplied are not the ones which were ordered. All of this leaves a great deal to be desired.
I seriously urge the minister, if he does not appreciate fully what is taking place here, to relinquish these activities by the Department of Defence Production for the purchase of materials for the Indian affairs branch and give those activities back to the proper minister who, in this instance, would be the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources. These activities should be returned to the Indian affairs branch which is intimately involved in the ordering of the materials and which will have the greatest amount of control in the placement of these orders. This will overcome a great deal of the difficulty.
I can assure the minister there is a fair amount of dissatisfaction within the Indian affairs branch in connection with this operation. If the Minister of Industry would just lean over and consult with the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources he would probably get confirmation of this dissatisfaction. I believe the minister should relinquish this activity because he has enough to do in this department without fiddling with the Indian affairs branch and causing a great deal of difficulty and inefficiency there.

Mr. Chairman, because the Minister and the government has decided to take positive action in the standards branch of the department relating to the problems of highway deaths and injuries, I wish to make a few remarks relating to the general subject. May I again congratulate the minister and the government upon the positive action which has been taken. As the minister announced in the house a few days ago in answer to written questions that I put on the order paper, the government intends to draft in the standards section of the Department of Defence Production a relatively definitive code pertaining to the purchase of government automobiles and to the safety features that should be included in motor cars at the production stage. I think that the Canadian public will be glad to receive the good news the Department of Defence Production has announced, namely that it intends to draft three codes for the public relating to the driver, to
Supply-Defence Production the car, and to the highway. Those three factors are obviously involved in highway deaths and injuries.
I do not intend to go into the great detail that I covered in the debate on the Speech from the Throne, but may I clear up some misconceptions. Many spokesmen for the industry and for the automobile establishment, for highway safety leagues, have stated up to now that I have placed too much emphasis on the car and not enough on the driver and on the highway. I have said that we must educate people to become better drivers; that we must encourage drivers to be more safe; that we must encourage provincial governments to build safer highways, and that we must encourage provincial governments to make sure that motorcars are operational at all times.
As a federal legislator there are some things which I may suggest. As federal legislators we can do something about what most members recognize to be an epidemic of massive proportions which has to be cured by massive public interest and massive public funds. That is what I said in the house before.
Unless something is done immediately, unless something is done to check the numbers killed on our highways, unless something is done between now and 1970, over a million Canadians will be injured and between 35,000 and 40,000 killed on our highways. What can we as federal legislators do about this. We can make certain that when the Canadian public buys an automobile that automobile is the safest that can be produced.
I have been criticized by some persons who say that I place the emphasis in the wrong place. I admit that apart from mechanical failure it should be recognized that judgment errors on the part of individuals are invariably responsible for an accident. However, as I keep saying to the leaders of the industry that after I have driven 80,000 miles, and just because I make a judgment error at a speed under 45 miles an hour, and just because the industry has not produced a safe automobile, is no reason for me to die.
As federal legislators, Mr. Chairman, if we support the initiative taken by the Department of Defence Production in the announcement of its code, if we support this worthy cause, it is my firm belief-and I draw the attention of the house to this at this time, -that we shall cut down the toll of deaths and injuries by 50 per cent.
I pointed out in the debate in the Speech from the Throne that 87 per cent of all

Defence Production deaths and injury-producing accidents take place at speeds under 45 miles an hour. This, Mr. Chairman, is something that we, as federal legislators can do something about.
There are those who pretend that we have no authority over the policing of safe motor cars. I say that the federal government has authority. May I direct your attention, Mr. Chairman, and the attention of the house to the Food and Drug Act. May I refer to the case of Russell v. The Queen. May I refer to the fact that the federal government has jurisdiction to police the manufacturing of aeroplanes, of all rolling stock on our railways, of all ships, and safety features in them, at production levels.
I should like to thank most sincerely the officials of the Department of Transport who, with the concurrence of the minister, put this working paper in my hands. It clearly demonstrates how at the production level the federal government has this authority in relation to planes, rolling stock on railways and the construction of ships to make sure that safety features are included for the protection of the public. These modes of communication and travel fall under the rule of law. The automobile alone falls outside the rule of law, and in the light of the few statistics I have put before the committee tonight I think it is incumbent upon us in a bipartisan spirit to conquer this epidemic which has now reached major proportions.
Some people approached me a few days ago and said that those of us who are working in this direction must be pleased by the announcement the industry made last week in connection with brakes and steering columns. I do not want to be a killjoy and say that these innovations are insignificant per se, but I believe that until we have government specified codes by which to measure the value of these innovations we have no means of knowing how significant they are.
Would we permit the food industry to say: "We are going to be good boys; we have taken a little poison out of our food"? We should want to know how much poison there was in it in the past and how much was left. Until we have these codified standards set by the authority which should make them, the public will not be protected.
The real reason for my intervention this evening is to congratulate the minister on the initiative he has taken in the Department of Defence Production. It is only a beginning. I can visualize the possibility, when the codes come out, that we shall need to do more than


hold them out to the automotive industry and say: "Be good boys; this is what we think you should do." We shall have to say: "We know these are scientific and proven safety features, and they must be in the cars within a definite period of time-or else."
Even if we do this we shall only be scratching the surface. The industry doubts whether we have authority to act in this field. It does not want to be policed. But if we are to do our duty to the public it will have to be policed. In the second place, the industry says we are setting back safety in general when we talk about the car and do not talk about the driver and the highway. I have already cleared up this point. The provincial governments have a definite role to play in helping to produce better drivers and in building safer highways. This does not mean we should avoid our responsibility at the federal level.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
The third argument that is being presented by the industry over the past few weeks is that they say if those who seek the building of a safer automobile want just that, they will build us an ugly tank that can go at 15 miles an hour. I would like to show members of the committee pictures of a prototype safety car that is being produced as a result of a feasibility study in New York. This is a safe car and a good looking car. How about the Pina Farina that is coming from Europe this year, which includes many safety features upon which no research is required, as they are already in existence?
It is patently obvious that you can build a good looking car and have safety features in it at the same time, and I think the minister's code and investigation will prove that. The industry says it cannot build us a good looking car and a safe car at the same time. I ask the industry, since when would proper rollover bars detract from beauty? Since when would properly recessed padded dash panels detract from the beauty of a car? Since when would integrating the seats of a car to the frame, so that they would not fly off at speeds under 45 miles an hour and cause great injury, detract from the beauty of a car? Since when would putting something stronger than cardboard between the rear end of a car and the valise, so that tools would not come in and cause injury and death, detract from the beauty of a car?
I put the following suggestions before the minister. First of all, I ask the minister would he plead with the automobile industry to
March 1. 1966

forgo costly retooling costs for style changes in the next year, and devote that money to putting safety in their automobiles.
Second, I have already talked about the New York prototype safety study, and I would say the state of New York is more advanced than any governmental body in the western world in the completion of a real safety car. The state has spent $500,000 on a feasibility study. They need from $4 million to $6 million to complete the building of a prototype car. It is interesting that the feasibility study was done by the aircraft industry. It is the aircraft industry which has spent millions and billions of dollars on research, while almost less than nothing has been spent, on automobile safety research.
I put the following suggestion before the minister: First of all, I ask:
What happened at Ste. Therese two years ago? An aircraft crashed and the government spent millions of dollars putting that aircraft back, piece by piece, and spent months studying it. We tried to find out why that tragedy occurred in order that we could do something about it. But what happens when a car crashes? We lose over 100 people a week on the highways; but after an accident, within 10 to 20 minutes of the ambulance or morgue wagon leaving the scene, the car involved is brought to the dump and not one dollar is spent on research to discover the cause.
It is the aircraft industry that has researched safety in automobiles. Therefore I would like to recommend to the minister the possibility that Canada could reach across the border, break precedent in many regards, if you will, and participate in a financial way in the building of the New York prototype car.
Though we have not reached the National Research Council aspect of the minister's estimates, I do feel that it could have a part to play in offering know-how in the completion of this prototype car. This is one instance where Canada can take a real lead in getting something done. If Canada takes the lead with New York and California, and one other large state, the major part of this war can be won. Can we expect much from Washington? The automobile lobby in Washington is very large and, as the minister knows, the G.S.A. recommendations were watered down last year because of that lobby. Canada must play its part.
Supply-Defence Production
The last recommendation which I put before the minister is that I hope the government will encourage its members, and opposition members, to have the house committee on research and industry call before it responsible leaders of the industry and research safety experts, so that in a spirit of co-operation we can get something done. I regret very much the outcry from the industry against me last week. I will not reply in kind to the executive who spoke the way he did, because I think this is too important a subject to get into a shouting match about.
Let us not allocate blame. I blame legislators such as ourselves for the state of affairs that we are faced with today regarding the problem; I blame the public because they have been so apathetic in demanding safety, and I blame the automobile industry also for being delinquent in their social and economic responsibilities. But let us not allocate blame; the blame is collective. Let us get on with the job and produce results. The last misconception I would like to shoot down is with respect to the safety experts. I am not sure what a safety expert is, but I tell the people in the industry that you do not need to be an employee of the industry to be an expert. The industry builds automobiles for people who are not experts; the five thousand people who died on our highways in 1965 were not experts, they were amateurs. These people are driving automobiles and the automobiles should be designed in a safe way so that they are adapted to the human animal. We should stop putting emphasis on the human animal always being adapted to the automobile.
What I am talking about will do two things: If we live up to our responsibilities and make sure that all scientifically proven safety features are put in cars at the production level, we will not only reduce death-producing and injury-producing accidents by 50 per cent, but we will also avoid many accidents occurring in the first place. I refer especially to such things as driver fatigue, and the basic research being done by the aircraft industry, on pilot fatigue, easily could be transferred to the automobile industry.
Great research has been done by the aircraft industry in matters relating to proper vision and noise, research which could avoid accidents in the first place. I am not talking about only reducing injury and death once the accident takes place, but also about the possibility of reducing the occurrence of the accident in the first place. While I am sure all
March 1, 1966

Supply-Defence Production members would agree that things such as high speed and drinking, pure bad driving and bad manners on the road, often are the cause of accidents, I do not think these things in themselves are an excuse for us to let the automobile as a mode of transportation go unpoliced.
I repeat that the problem is too great for us to just shunt off our responsibilities in this manner. President Johnson a couple of weeks ago when referring to the matter in Washington said that the whole problem of highway death and injury, came second only to the problem of Viet Nam, and suggested that surely this means we have a role to play in overcoming the problem.
I would like to congratulate the minister for his initial thrust and initiative in tackling the problem, and I would like to ask all the members of the house to pledge their support to him when we move into this area.

Mr. Chairman, had we proceeded some 15 minutes ago I would have finished my remarks by now. I think it is a well known fact that I have had many questions on the order paper with regard to the Canadian Government Printing Bureau. It is also a well known fact to me that I have received some very left-handed answers to these questions and there are some 20 question to which I have not yet received any answer.
I should like to say that I am not on a witch hunt; I am not seeking to aggravate French-English relations within the bureau, which I know personally to be on the most unhappy of all bases. In my opinion the situation within the government printing bureau warrants, indeed demands, a thoroughgoing public inquiry. I am deeply disturbed by the situation that I know to exist and I have reason to believe that the minister also is much more concerned than he will admit to this house.
I have had a whole series of questions on the order paper seeking to elicit detailed information on the bureau operation, employment practices and inventory procedures, all with a view to establishing the fact that the Canadian taxpayer is indeed getting value for his tax dollar. I have been bombarded with a mass of ministerial white paper which promises to tell much but which, in reality, discloses very little. I said, Mr. Chairman, that I was not engaged in a witch hunt and I meant precisely that. It matters not a whit to me whether anyone attributes the real situation that exists in the bureau to the years the present government has been in office or to any other administration. My own,

DEBATES	March 1. 1966
fundamental concern is to eradicate from the bureau, which bears the proud title of the Queen's Printer, practices that I am fully convinced are mulcting the Canadian public of thousands and thousands of dollars annually.
My information is that over the years there have been illegitimate practices at the bureau involving shortages of stock, the use of or outright theft of bureau equipment and supplies for private gain of certain individuals. My information further is that within the internal operation of the bureau there has been rank discrimination against certain personnel. My inquiries have revealed the operation of an illicit lending agency, group or society or what you might wish to call a Caisse Populaire. I have heard this described as a loan shark business. I say to the minister, this is just not good enough. This is deplorable, and is a situation which cannot be tolerated within an agency of the Crown.
Proof that the case I am submitting to the committee is not a witch hunt, Mr. Chairman, is provided by acknowledgements from the minister himself in some replies to my questions to the effect that the R.C.M.P., and the Hull city police have been compelled to carry their investigations into the theft of television sets, radios, tape recorders or other equipment into the bureau itself. My information is also that the city police of Ottawa have had a hand in these investigations. Indeed, in one instance, they seized a television set in the possession of a bureau employee.
The minister's response to my series of questions was beyond criticism for volume, but left much to be desired in the way of providing specific answers to specific questions. I can only conclude that he does not provide these answers in detail because of the danger of embarrassing himself and the government.
It seems to be the custom of employees of the Canadian Government Printing Bureau to become connected with outside enterprises, the work of which is allied to their line of work in the bureau. I will cite three or four cases, but I am going to refrain from naming individuals in so far as I can do so. I am not interested in castigating anyone, only in protecting the rights of the Canadian taxpayer. My information indicates the existence of the following examples:
A man who is a full time photographer within the bureau operates his own photography business outside of the bureau and has

access to equipment and supplies within the bureau.
The firm of Gasparo Limited, a commercial printing firm located in Hull, according to the answer given to question No. 329, is operated by at least a dozen employees of the bureau, three of whom are listed as directors of that company. The answer also relates that they have a 60 per cent interest in this business. I am further informed that 40 per cent is held in the name of a Hull businessman, as a front to keep the employees out of trouble.
I am further advised that this man either received a lump sum or an annual fee or dividend to protect these people.
It has also come to my attention that shortly after the first questions were asked, some of these people in the bureau worked long and hard removing equipment, etc. from these premises. I should think that an investigational committee would want to know what equipment was moved; where did it come from; where is it now? I am sure these answers would be very revealing.
I can also see two of these foremen, whom I could name, meeting in the Printing Bureau that evening, shaking hands and feeling that they have covered their tracks.
Further, No. 3, my impression of Accurate Printing, according to my informants, in spite of left-handed and evasive answers to question No. 327 is that one, Mr. A. R. Gentile was employed by the Printing Bureau until October 12, 1965, at which time he was a hand compositor. During this same period he operated a firm known as Accurate Printing, 12 Kevin Crescent, Ottawa. I am informed that this work was done at the bureau, perhaps on bureau printing time, and perhaps using printing bureau equipment and material. To sum it all up, Mr. Chairman, my inquiries have revealed very definite wrongdoing in the Canadian Government Printing Bureau. First, there are three firms, all owned and operated by employees of the Canadian Government Printing Bureau, and interested in allied trades. These employees had access to equipment and supplies which could be used in their own, private business. Two of these firms have received government contracts.
Second, there is information that a money lending syndicate has operated and may still be operating within the bureau, and is doing business with the less fortunate at exorbitant interest rates in excess of 100 per cent.
Third, I have been informed that a ring has been operating in selling television, radios, tape recorders, etc., at ridiculously low prices at printing bureau premises to printing bureau employees. I am further informed that a television set was seized by Ottawa police from the home of a printing bureau employee and has not yet been returned.
How many other operations there are only a complete investigation would bring to light. I am informed that there are many.

I should like to know this, Mr. Chairman. What were those items in detail? Did they not have some salvage value? Why were they not turned over to Crown Assets Disposal Corporation? Surely something could have been saved. Or was this representative of an inventory shortage; was this an attempt to cover up? What about other shortages in the inventory? Mr. Chairman, I am not interested in ruining the career of any individual, hence my hesitation about mentioning names. But I am interested in protecting the Canadian taxpayer. I am not approaching this matter in a partisan way. I am happy to let the chips fall where they may. If part of this situation can be traced to the previous administration, so be it. We are interested only in seeing that this situation is cleared up.
The onus is directly on the minister. Nothing will satisfy me or the people of Canada short of a public inquiry. Or we might turn the whole messy business over to a parliamentary committee composed of representatives of all parties in the house. I would personally supply to such a committee a list of some 30 or 40 witnesses to be called.

At this late hour I do not intend to make any extensive comments. However, I do wish to make some reference to the Department of Industry more particularly in connection with the government's designated area policy.
First I think it is necessary to mention the historic apathy felt by the Liberal party toward policies relating to the Atlantic area. This is the basic problem as I see it. In the 22 years up to 1957 we in the Atlantic area were retarded because the government of the day did not appreciate the fact that special policies, and a special application of national policies had to be considered as far as the maritime provinces were concerned.
Because of this we were not able to move forward. When a Conservative government

was elected in 1957 in Ottawa, consideration was given to the special problems of the Atlantic area, and legislation was passed which had an immediate impact, and continues to have an impact on the economy of the area.
The minister has indicated that the government will continue to look at the Atlantic area in just the same way as it looks at the province of Ontario or the province of Saskatchewan, with respect to the area development program and the selection of designated areas. Everybody who has an appreciation of the problems in the Atlantic area has requested the minister to designate the whole area, but he has continuously refused to do this and says the program will apply in the Atlantic provinces in the same way as in other parts of Canada.
One of the best examples why this does not work is to compare a designated area in Ontario, which is surrounded by non-desig-nated areas. Immediately there is an attraction to it from the areas not designated, so that in a short time its designation can be removed, but it will still be able to attract industries from the surrounding areas. This does not happen to be the case in the Atlantic provinces.
In the Atlantic provinces we have three or four growth areas, the rest being designateed. Our problem is that we must first create the right kind of atmosphere in the areas of affluence, if one wishes to call them that, so that benefits will flow from those areas into the other surplus labour areas, and so that surplus labour may be attracted into the affluent areas.
The minister has adopted the attitude that he does not want any change made in his program. He says it is going to apply the same way in B.C. as in Newfoundland, but surely he is coming to realize that things are not the same in the Atlantic provinces? If he is not, then he should go beyond the borders of Quebec and get some appreciation of what our problems are.
Just a few days ago in the provincial legislature, Premier Stanfield condemned the federal government because it was not willing to listen to the proposal that the whole Atlantic area be designated, and the special assistance granted under it be made available no matter where an industry might wish to locate in the Atlantic provinces. If the Minister of Industry does not know now that Premier Stanfield has the best possible appreciation of how to improve the economic

climate in Nova Scotia, he never will because, as he should be aware, this was one of the basic arguments in Nova Scotia during the federal election campaign.

The Minister of National Health and Wei-fare adopted the attitude he adopts in so far as the Atlantic provinces are concerned, adopted the attitude which his government adopts, and surely the result on November 8 is the best indication in the world of where the people of Nova Scotia put their confidence in so far as progress is concerned. Surely this government is interested in the seats in Nova Scotia, and is interested in improving their position there in the days ahead, because if redistribution comes into effect, under the existing conditions and the existing recommendations, the Liberal party as it stands at the present time is going to be left without one representative from that area, unless they are able to convince somebody in that province that they are realistic in their policies and that their policies are going to have some benefit.
In the Conservative party we even have taken the approach, if the minister cannot do what we ask within the confines of this legislation, that it should be done through the Atlantic Development Board, a board set up specifically to take into consideration situations such as this. But the Minister of Transport, who is answerable to the House of Commons for the Atlantic Development Board, certainly indicated in no uncertain terms to the member for Saint John-Albert that the Atlantic Development Board was not going to become involved in this matter, and that it is a matter which is being left at the door of the Minister of Industry.
I say to the Minister of Industry that his policy as it presently applies to the Atlantic provinces is not good enough; it is not good enough for the Premier of Nova Scotia, it is not good enough for the people of Nova Scotia, and I am sure that applies in any given area in the Atlantic region. I ask him again to re-consider a decision in respect of a policy which may be very satisfactory in some areas of Canada but is most unsatisfactory in the Atlantic area.
When you take a body like the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council, which for years has been studying how to improve prospects with regard to the attraction of industry and the elimination of high unemployment, and
Supply-Defence Production which presently is very much in existence in our area, you will get some appreciation of the kind of policies which should apply. This body has been urging the minister and this government for some time to designate the whole of the Atlantic provinces, and not leave out Halifax, Dartmouth, Saint John and Frederiction, and make sure that we do nothing to hinder this kind of growth that is needed in this area so that we will be able to attract to the whole of the area, to any part of the area, the industry that we must have if we are to eradicate the high unemployment that is so very evident there at the present time.
I say to the minister, never mind being a bureaucrat, like he once was; never mind being so difficult that when he once has made a decision he will say it never can be changed. Just give the kind of consideration that will be of benefit to our area, through this program. If he will do this, I am sure he will get full marks for it. The first man who would commend the government for its action would be the Premier of Nova Scotia, who I believe stands second to none in his knowledge concerning how new industry best can be attracted to our area, the problems associated with high unemployment and how they can be eliminated.

Mr. Chairman, I too, want to say a word or two about designated areas and the criteria used to set them up, as carried forward by the Department of Industry. I realize that time is quickly passing and I will not go into this whole subject of diversification and decentralization of industry, about which I have spoken on many other occasions. However, I feel this is very important to a young country such as Canada is today.

This is a big subject which we have not time enough to go into tonight. We want to know about the area development program mentioned here through the designated area legislation. No matter what happens with respect to that, you are in trouble. If you move the line from here to there, you are still in trouble. Ever since this legislation has been brought in it has been nothing but discriminatory from beginning to end. I had experience in the early days of it. One of my first experiences with it was when Brantford was made a designated area, and the city of Guelph was not. speechtext:
I do not doubt that I shall be one of the most unpopular members of this committee for a few minutes but I believe national research is a subject on which some comment should be made. I feel sure that in a country such as ours there is no more important thing for the future than research. It is on this basis that I make these few comments.
Two or three weeks ago I asked the Prime Minister a question about the amount of research money which is coming to us from the United States. Unfortunately, the information which Dr. Polanyi gave in the course of a broadcast dealing with the subject was not quite correct and the Prime Minister pointed this out. Nevertheless the fact remains that there is a substantial amount of money coming to us from the United States for use in research. I fear we shall lose much of this money as a result of restrictions in connection with the transfer of funds from the United States to Canada. This makes it imperative in my view that we should increase our research grants.
I know that a great deal could be said about the subject but it is my intention to be brief. I hope the minister when presenting his estimates for the coming year will take this matter into consideration and see that his colleagues increase substantially the grants
[(Mr. Hales.]
which are made to the National Research Council and to the Medical Research Council.
There are many points I could bring out to support this contention, but time is short. However, I want to illustrate what is happening by referring to the two gentlemen who were mentioned on the broadcast to which I have referred, Dr. Bartlett from the University of British Columbia and Dr. Polanyi of the University of Toronto, who made the broadcast. Dr. Bartlett, I am afraid, is leaving for Princeton though other universities in Canada have done their best to keep him here. Since he has won not only the Steacie award but another award, the research corporation award for 1965, worth $10,000, he is obviously the kind of man we would like to keep in Canada. If we are to do this we must not only see that these men are well paid, we must see they get the students who can work with them, places in which to live and the equipment necessary for them to carry out the research they want to do.
Much of it may seem to be research that does not mean anything, but in the long run often means a great deal. We need the buildings which will accommodate this research, so I make a plea to the minister to see that in his new estimates full consideration is given to this fact, so that research grants will be greatly enlarged, and I mean greatly enlarged.
The best estimate the Canadian Association of Graduate Schools was able to come up with was that expenditures should be $160 million a year by 1970-71, and over $250 million a year by 1975. These are almost astronomical figures in relation to what is being done today, but I hope this will be given the fullest consideration and that more generous grants will be made.

speechtext:
Earlier this evening we had some discussion on designated areas, which the minister said were designated because they contained so little industry and had such high unemployment that the government felt something should be done about the situation. I suggest we are reaching a point where there are other areas in the country which should
March 1, 1966

be designated because of the fact that they contain so much industry that they are reaching the stage where they are no longer fit for people to live and work in them.
This is because industry has been allowed to develop in a way that its operations create pollution of the air and neighbouring waters, pollution which is reaching an acute danger point so far as the welfare of people is concerned.
I discussed this matter for a few minutes the other night when the estimates of the Department of Forestry were before us, with particular reference to one research item. Also, as the Minister of Industry may have noted, I have a question on the order paper, but apparently I am not alone in that, in attempting to find out what the federal government is doing through its various agencies in the field of research into air and water pollution.
So far as I am aware, the National Research Council is the most important research organism in the whole establishment of the federal government, and this item of the estimates is of interest to me.
I have noted a resolution on the order paper respecting certain changes in the operation, as well as the title of the research council. I am sure the government house leader is anxious that that resolution be discussed at the earliest possible date. However, one of the reasons I am rising tonight is to draw to the attention of the minister the fact that my question has been on the order paper since February 9, and to say I hope I shall receive an answer to it before we come to deal with the resolution preceding legislation respecting the National Research Council. I am referring to question No. 555, and I hope I receive the answer before we come to discuss what the future nature of the federal government's research activities should be.
[DOT] (12 midnight)
I am not going to pursue this question at any length tonight, except to say that I would appreciate it very much if the minister could, out of hand, name for me any of the major efforts presently under way by the National Research Council in the field of air pollution research or water pollution research, if such in fact do exist.
